name: Orokaiva
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_quote: The first syllable of each Orokaiva word is stressed. When h occurs between unstressed vowels it is very light, and sometimes seems to be quite silent.

new_statements.quote: Stress is non-phonemic. The primary stress is always on the first syllable of each word. If the first two syllables involve the sequence Va, then the second syllable sometimes seems to be nearly as prominent as the first one. In reduplicated and compound words a secondary stress occurs on the first syllable of the second root. In simple words a secondary stress tends to occur on the third syllable, but it is not easily heard if that syllable does not contain a stop or /a/.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not phonemic; primary stress falls on the first syllable of every word. A secondary stress falls on the third syllable in simple words (weakly audible unless that syllable has a stop or /a/) and on the first syllable of the second root in reduplicated and compound words. When the first two syllables form a V-a sequence the second syllable can sound nearly as prominent as the first.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Simple words: secondary stress tends to fall on the third syllable, hard to hear unless that syllable contains a stop or /a/. Reduplicated and compound words: secondary stress on the first syllable of the second root.
new_statements.exceptions: No exceptions to initial primary stress; only the remark that in an initial V-a sequence the second syllable can sound almost as prominent as the first. Section 5.2 adds that vowels in monosyllables and stressed syllables tend to be lengthened.
new_statements.identity_note: Larsen & Larsen 1977 is the SIL description of Orokaiva proper (the same authors and the same language as the 1982 lessons volume); no dialect is named in the excerpt or in the phonology's stress section.

sources.quote: Stress is always on the first syllable of Orokaiva words of more than one syllable with secondary stress on the third syllable of words longer than three syllables. Therefore since stress is so predictable it is a good indicator of word boundaries. Consider the stress as marked in the following examples. na ém.bo ta íñ.da.ri úm.bu-to pám.ba.só-n-a 'I will take the man's food and go.' The primary stress on em- of ém.bo shows a word break between na and em; also between ta and in-, between -to and pam- and secondary stress on -so- of pám.ba.só.na ties it together as one word.
